standard: Structures this project researched and deliberately left out of this scene, with the evidence that dates them. It is not a list of everything missing: most of the town is simply not built yet.

excluded.name: Saloon Building
excluded.detail: South-east corner Clark and Lake; three-story brick, erected 1836 by Capt. J. B. F. Russell and George W. Doan. Chicago's first three-story structure and the largest hall west of Buffalo; the city charter was received here in 1837 and it served as City Hall to 1842.

excluded.detail: North-west corner Clark and Randolph; large three-story brick, built by Francis C. Sherman.

excluded.reason: Built 1836, and well outside the platted town in any case.
excluded.detail: Greek Revival on 20 acres near what is now Michigan Ave and 16th St. Frequently and wrongly pulled into early-Chicago scenes because it survives today as the city's oldest house.

excluded.detail: Frame building on the north side of Lake Street near Wells, two stories with eaves to the street. High uncertainty — excluded on the balance of evidence rather than a firm date.

excluded.reason: Built 1837 — the first brick house erected in Chicago.
excluded.detail: Peck in 1835 was living at his two-story frame store at the south-west corner of South Water and LaSalle. His LaSalle and Washington dwelling appears in an 1837 description. Model Peck at the store.

excluded.reason: The town's first fire engine was purchased 1 December 1835 for $894.38 — five months AFTER the scene date.
excluded.detail: A tidy example of why the date gate matters: 1835 is the right year and still the wrong scene.

excluded.name: Frink & Walker stage office
excluded.reason: Appears only in later material. In 1835-36 stage seats were taken at Markle's Exchange Coffee House at Lake and Wells — there is no separate stage-office building yet.

excluded.name: G. S. Hubbard's South Water Street packing house
excluded.reason: Dates to 1840; his Kinzie Street packing house is 1837-38.
excluded.detail: In 1834 Hubbard packed in the old bank building at Lake and LaSalle. Any 1835 Hubbard warehouse on South Water is unsupported — 'Hubbard's Folly' does not appear in Andreas at all.

excluded.name: Pier-head light at the end of the North Pier
excluded.reason: A later structure; the skeletal iron pier light dates to 1859.
excluded.detail: The light standing in 1835 is the second tower, forty feet high, begun and completed by Samuel Jackson in 1832 and modelled as data/structures/chicago_lighthouse_1832.json. Do not put a light on the pier. AMENDED 2026-08-11: this entry previously called that tower 'the 1832 conical masonry tower' on Andreas's authority. Andreas's sentence gives the 1832 tower a height, a builder and a reflector and no shape and no material; 'The walls were three feet thick' and the fifty-foot height in the same paragraph belong to the FIRST tower, which fell unfinished on 30 October 1831. An exclusion should guard a boundary, not carry an attribution its sources do not support on the way past.

excluded.name: John Kinzie House (the old Kinzie mansion)
excluded.reason: GONE by the scene date — documented absence, not a date guard.
excluded.detail: The du Sable/Kinzie house on the north bank opposite the fort was unoccupied and 'dilapidated beyond repair' from 1832 and reported gone by 1835. The commemorative plaque dates it 1784-1832. Note that the Conley/Stelzer 1933 map labels it 'Old Kinzie Mansion, built 1832', which contradicts every documentary source — a good illustration of why a tier-5 reconstruction is never sole evidence. The two large cottonwoods behind the house are separately attested and one survived into the 20th century, so the TREES belong in the 1835 scene even though the house does not.

excluded.name: Antoine Ouilmette's cabin
excluded.reason: Almost certainly gone — Ouilmette left for Gross Pointe in the later 1820s and no source attests the cabin's survival past that decade.
excluded.detail: It belonged to the Kinzie mansion group, which was derelict by 1832. Omit, or model as a ruin at most, and only with better evidence than currently exists.

excluded.name: Methodist Episcopal church, south side
excluded.reason: LOCATION guard rather than a date guard. The Methodist meeting house was NOT on the south side in 1835 — the congregation floated it across the river and rolled it on logs to Clark and Washington only in 1838. Which bank it was on BEFORE that move is disputed and this entry no longer asserts it: see data/structures/walker_meeting_house.json, where the west-bank and north-bank readings are set out and the position is tagged conjectural. The guard holds either way, because both candidate banks are north or west of the south division.
excluded.detail: The 'M.E. Church' shown south of the river on the 1833 reconstructed map is best read as showing where Methodists met — the fort, and later the Temple Building — not a Methodist-owned building. The brick Clark Street church is 1844. Amended 2026-08-09: this entry previously stated the north bank as settled fact, which contradicted the structure record written against the same evidence. An exclusion should guard a boundary, not quietly decide an open question on the way past.

excluded.name: Lake House hotel (completed)
excluded.reason: Ground was broken in 1835 but it opened in the fall of 1836.
excluded.detail: On the scene date this is a CONSTRUCTION SITE, not a building — a partial three-story brick shell on the north bank at Rush and Kinzie. It should be modelled in that state as a structure phase, not excluded outright; this entry exists to stop the finished hotel appearing.

citations.citation: "A Chronology of Early Chicago Area Hotels." Digital Research Library of Illinois History Journal.

excluded.name: The first Fort Dearborn (1803–1812)
excluded.reason: Burned by the Pottawatomie on 16 August 1812, the day after the evacuation and the massacre. It is not a date guard so much as a SOURCE guard: most of what is published about 'Fort Dearborn's' plan describes this fort and gets applied to the one standing in 1835.
excluded.detail: Captain John Whistler built it in 1803 and drew a measured plan of it in 1808 which survives in the War Department files and is printed with its index by Quaife. That fort had TWO BLOCKHOUSES at the south-east and north-west angles, a DOUBLE ROW OF PICKETS with the blockhouses commanding the space between them, a COVERED WAY or SALLY-PORT to the river, a FLAGSTAFF in the parade, barracks two storeys high with GALLERIES fronting the parade, and THREE PIECES OF LIGHT ARTILLERY. The second fort, rebuilt on the same ground in 1816, had ONE blockhouse at the south-west and bastions at the north-west and south-east, and John H. Kinzie says in terms that the two were 'differently constructed'. The passage that carries most of the first fort's description in the popular literature closes with the sentence 'Such was the old Fort previous to 1812'. Everything in this entry is excluded from 1835 and none of it may be borrowed for the second fort's records.

excluded.name: Fort Dearborn's sally-port (subterranean passage to the river)
excluded.reason: A FIRST-FORT feature, wrongly carried into this project's own dossier as attested for the 1816 fort.
excluded.detail: 'On the north side a subterranean passage, leading from the parade ground to the river, designed as a place of escape in an emergency, or for supplying the garrison with water in time of a siege' - Andreas, in his description of the fort built in 1803, and repeated in the Chicago Magazine of March 1857 in a passage that ends 'Such was the old Fort previous to 1812'. Whistler's own 1808 index lists it as 'N. 33 Covered Way to procure Water'. John H. Kinzie names it as one of the ways the first fort DIFFERED from the second. docs/research/04-structures-south.md section 1.2 tags it [DOC] 'attested for the 1816 fort's north side'; that reading is not supported by the page it cites, and no source reached attests a sally-port at the second fort. Not modelled.

excluded.name: A hospital building inside Fort Dearborn
excluded.reason: NO SUCH BUILDING IS ATTESTED. The hospital in the sources is a USE of the fort during the 1832 cholera, not a structure in it.
excluded.detail: The War Department return quoted in Wentworth's address reads 'Fort Dearborn having become a general hospital on July 11th [1832], no returns were received until its reoccupation' - the whole post was given over to sick troops off General Scott's steamers, and the officers and their families 'took shelter wherever they could'. That is an emergency use in July 1832 and by 1835 it has lapsed. docs/research/04-structures-south.md section 1.2 lists a 'hospital' among the fort's buildings tagged [DOC] from that page; there is no hospital building on it. The U.S. Marine Hospital that appears in the 1855 photograph caption is the vantage point of the photograph, built on the reservation after an appropriation of 1848, and is neither a fort building nor within twenty years of the scene date.

excluded.name: Fort Dearborn's whitewashed board fence, turnstile and 400-foot parade
excluded.reason: The compound of the 1850s, after the pickets came down and the army left. A LATER-STATE guard rather than a date guard on a building.
excluded.detail: Robert Fergus, describing the fort in 1850: 'The whole Fort enclosure was surrounded by a rough-board fence, white-washed, about 6 feet high; the pickets having been removed at an earlier date', with a turnstile entering from the centre of Michigan Avenue about 100 ft south of the sun-dial knoll, and a parade ground 'about 80 feet wide' running 'from the river bank south, the full length of the enclosure - say 400 feet'. NONE of that describes 1835: the pickets are attested standing by Juliette Kinzie in 1831 and drawn on the 1830 plan, the post was garrisoned until 29 December 1836, and the reservation was unplatted in 1835 so Michigan Avenue did not commence at that point. The fort is modelled stockaded. The sun-dial itself is carried back into the scene on the record data/structures/fort_dearborn_parade.json, which says so on the attribute; the fence, the turnstile and the 400 ft parade are not.

excluded.name: The fort's three pieces of light artillery
excluded.reason: Attested for the FIRST fort and for no other date. A guard on fort furniture, which the dossiers carry as though it were 1835-relevant.
excluded.detail: 'The Fort was furnished with three pieces of light-artillery' and 'A company of United-States troops, about fifty in number, many of whom were invalids, constituted the garrison' both stand in the Chicago Magazine passage that ends 'Such was the old Fort previous to 1812'. docs/research/08-fauna.md takes the fifty invalids from that page as 1835-relevant. Nothing reached says what ordnance stood at the second fort at any date; an artillery HOUSE is named once, in a description of the fort in 1850, and is modelled as data/structures/fort_dearborn_artillery_house.json with the guns left out. No gun is drawn anywhere in this scene.
